claim: The mammalian master circadian clock is localized within the hypothalamic suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN).
source: The mammalian master circadian clock is localized within the hypothalamic suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), where nearly 20,000 neurons synchronize their daily activity with the light-dark cycle to orchestrate circadian rhythms in physiology and behavior (Reppert and Weaver, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Reppert and Weaver, 2002

claim: Nearly 20,000 neurons in the SCN synchronize their daily activity with the light-dark cycle to orchestrate circadian rhythms in physiology and behavior.
source: The mammalian master circadian clock is localized within the hypothalamic suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), where nearly 20,000 neurons synchronize their daily activity with the light-dark cycle to orchestrate circadian rhythms in physiology and behavior (Reppert and Weaver, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Reppert and Weaver, 2002

claim: Most, if not all, SCN neurons contain an internal molecular clock that operates on a transcription-translation feedback loop (TTFL).
source: Most, if not all, SCN neurons contain an internal molecular clock that operates on a transcription-translation feedback loop (TTFL) (Ko and Takahashi, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ko and Takahashi, 2006

claim: Activity of the TTFL drives circadian rhythms in electrical activity, with SCN neurons notably more active during the day (up-state) than at night (down-state).
source: Activity of the TTFL drives circadian rhythms in electrical activity, with SCN neurons notably more active during the day (up-state) than at night (down-state).
evidence: Draws from established scientific consensus about SCN neuronal activity patterns

claim: Current understanding of SCN neurophysiology comes overwhelmingly from electrophysiological recordings on a small number of nocturnal rodent species (mice, rats, and hamsters).
source: Our current understanding of SCN neurophysiology comes overwhelmingly from electrophysiological recordings on a small number of nocturnal rodent species (mice, rats, and hamsters) (Colwell, 2011; Belle and Diekman, 2018; Harvey et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Colwell, 2011; Belle and Diekman, 2018; Harvey et al., 2020

claim: The daytime peak in spontaneous action potential firing activity is retained in the SCN of diurnal species.
source: A handful of studies have confirmed that the daytime peak in spontaneous action potential firing activity (as reflected in extracellular electrical activity or deoxyglucose uptake) is retained in the SCN of diurnal species (Sato and Kawamura, 1984; Schwartz, 1991; Ruby and Heller, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sato and Kawamura, 1984; Schwartz, 1991; Ruby and Heller, 1996

claim: There have been no whole-cell recordings of SCN neurons from a diurnal species prior to this study.
source: To date, there have been no whole-cell recordings of SCN neurons from a diurnal species, and the question of how, or if, SCN neurophysiology is altered to accommodate a diurnal lifestyle remains unanswered.
evidence: Statement about the state of the field prior to this work

claim: Rhabdomys pumilio is primarily day-active.
source: This species is primarily day-active (Dewsbury and Dawson, 1979; Schumann et al., 2005; Mallarino et al., 2018; Bano-Otalora et al., 2021), and is a murid rodent, facilitating comparison with established findings from closely related nocturnal species (mice and rats).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dewsbury and Dawson, 1979; Schumann et al., 2005; Mallarino et al., 2018; Bano-Otalora et al., 2021

claim: R. pumilio is a murid rodent, facilitating comparison with established findings from closely related nocturnal species (mice and rats).
source: This species is primarily day-active (Dewsbury and Dawson, 1979; Schumann et al., 2005; Mallarino et al., 2018; Bano-Otalora et al., 2021), and is a murid rodent, facilitating comparison with established findings from closely related nocturnal species (mice and rats).
evidence: Statement about taxonomic classification and its implications for comparative studies

claim: R. pumilio has several visual system adaptations (cone rich retina, UV blocking lens) that are typical of animals relying on daytime vision.
source: The designation of R. pumilio as a reliably day-active species is supported by other aspects of its biology, particularly its visual system which has several adaptations (cone rich retina, UV blocking lens) that are typical of animals relying on daytime vision (Allen et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Allen et al., 2020

claim: The gross neuroanatomy of the R. pumilio SCN across the rostro-caudal axis is broadly similar to other rodent species.
source: The gross neuroanatomy of the R. pumilio SCN across the rostro-caudal axis is broadly similar to other rodent species (Smale and Boverhof, 1999; Abrahamson and Moore, 2001; Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citations to Smale and Boverhof, 1999; Abrahamson and Moore, 2001 and Figure 1A

claim: The R. pumilio SCN contains VIP, AVP, and GRP neuropeptides.
source: Immunofluorescence labeling for the main neuropeptides showed that the R. pumilio SCN contains VIP, AVP, and GRP, and importantly, the neuroanatomical localization of these neuropeptides was broadly similar to the distribution found in other rodent species (Smale and Boverhof, 1999; Abrahamson and Moore, 2001)
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data and citations to Smale and Boverhof, 1999; Abrahamson and Moore, 2001

claim: AVP-positive cell bodies in R. pumilio SCN were mainly localized in the dorsomedial aspect.
source: AVP-positive cell bodies were mainly localized in the dorsomedial aspect (sometimes termed 'shell' (Figure 1B))
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1B

claim: VIP-positive somas in R. pumilio SCN were localized throughout the ventral region or 'core', with VIP immunoreactive axonal processes extended into the dorsal SCN.
source: while VIP-positive somas were localized throughout the ventral region or 'core', with VIP immunoreactive axonal processes extended into the dorsal SCN (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1C

claim: GRP-positive neurons in R. pumilio SCN were localized in the central SCN.
source: By contrast, GRP-positive neurons were localized in the central SCN (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1D

claim: A total of 111 SCN neurons from eight R. pumilio animals were recorded over the day-night cycle.
source: Recording (Figure 2A) from a total of 111 SCN neurons (from eight animals) over the day-night cycle revealed several spontaneous excitability states in R. pumilio (Figure 2B)
evidence: Statement about the experimental sample size

claim: R. pumilio SCN neurons exhibit several spontaneous excitability states similar to previous descriptions in mice.
source: Recording (Figure 2A) from a total of 111 SCN neurons (from eight animals) over the day-night cycle revealed several spontaneous excitability states in R. pumilio (Figure 2B), similar to previous descriptions in mice (Belle et al., 2009; Diekman et al., 2013; Paul et al., 2016; Collins et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 2B and citations to Belle et al., 2009; Diekman et al., 2013; Paul et al., 2016; Collins et al., 2020

claim: Some R. pumilio SCN neurons were resting at moderate RMPs (−43.9 ±0.41 mV, n=94/111) and firing action potentials.
source: Thus, some SCN neurons were resting at moderate RMPs (−43.9 ±0.41 mV, n=94/111) and firing action potentials (APs).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements

claim: Some R. pumilio SCN neurons were severely depolarized or 'hyperexcited' (−32.7 ± 2.36, n=6/111).
source: Other neurons were severely depolarized or 'hyperexcited' (−32.7 ± 2.36, n=6/111), to the extent that rather than generating APs, they became depolarized-silent or exhibited depolarized low-amplitude membrane oscillations (DLAMOs).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements

claim: Some R. pumilio SCN neurons were hyperpolarized-silent, having RMPs too negative to sustain firing (−50.5 ± 2.29 mV, n=11/111).
source: The final category of neurons were hyperpolarized-silent, having RMPs too negative to sustain firing (−50.5 ± 2.29 mV, n=11/111).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements

claim: R. pumilio SCN neurons were overall more excited during the day than at night.
source: SCN neurons were overall more excited during the day than at night (Figure 2C–E), with hyperpolarized-silent neurons appearing at night, and the daytime state being characterized by firing and depolarized cells, indicating a time-of-day control on these cellular electrical states (χ2=21.498, p<0.001, Chi-square test, Figure 2C)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C-E and statistical analysis (χ2=21.498, p<0.001)

claim: RMP and SFR showed a robust circadian variation in R. pumilio SCN neurons.
source: Accordingly, RMP and SFR showed a robust circadian variation (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D-E

claim: During the day, R. pumilio SCN neurons were overall resting at more depolarized RMP, generating APs at a higher rate.
source: During the day, SCN neurons were overall resting at more depolarized RMP, generating APs at a higher rate.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements

claim: Cellular RMP in the diurnal R. pumilio SCN is a strong determinant of electrical states and SFR.
source: This indicates that, as in nocturnal species (Belle et al., 2009; Belle and Piggins, 2017), cellular RMP in the diurnal R. pumilio SCN is a strong determinant of electrical states and SFR.
evidence: Inference from experimental data and comparison with citations to Belle et al., 2009; Belle and Piggins, 2017

claim: R. pumilio SCN neurons could be driven to transit from the depolarized- through to hyperpolarized-silent states by progressive steps of steady-state suppressive currents.
source: Indeed, R. pumilio SCN neurons could be easily driven to transit from the depolarized- through to hyperpolarized-silent states, switching to DLAMOs and firing activity at appropriate RMPs in the process (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G

claim: Rinput values in R. pumilio SCN neurons showed a range from 0.84 to 4.47 GΩ, skewed toward high values.
source: Measurement of Rinput values showed a range from 0.84 to 4.47 GΩ, skewed toward high values, as reported in other species (Pennartz et al., 1998; Jackson et al., 2004; Kuhlman and McMahon, 2004; Belle et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements and citations to Pennartz et al., 1998; Jackson et al., 2004; Kuhlman and McMahon, 2004; Belle et al., 2009

claim: There was no significant day-night variation in Rinput in R. pumilio SCN neurons (F(1, 5.984)=0.878 p=0.385).
source: However, we found neither a significant day-night variation in this measure (F(1, 5.984)=0.878 p=0.385, Figure 2F)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and data shown in Figure 2F

claim: There was no correlation between Rinput and RMP in R. pumilio SCN neurons (R² = 0.0305, p=0.0695, n=109).
source: nor a correlation with RMP (R² = 0.0305, p=0.0695, n=109), which stands in contrast to measurements in the SCN of nocturnal animals (de Jeu et al., 1998; Kuhlman and McMahon, 2004; Belle et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and comparison with citations to de Jeu et al., 1998; Kuhlman and McMahon, 2004; Belle et al., 2009

claim: The lack of correlation between Rinput and RMP represents the first substantial difference between R. pumilio and mouse or rat SCN.
source: This represents the first substantial difference between R. pumilio and mouse or rat SCN.
evidence: Inference from comparison of experimental results with previous literature

claim: A small proportion of R. pumilio SCN neurons (21/102) responded to depolarizing pulses with a sustained and regular train of action potentials, with no, or marginal, spike-frequency adaptation (non-adapting cells).
source: When subjected to depolarizing pulses, R. pumilio SCN neurons exhibited electrical responses similar to those of nocturnal species: a small proportion of cells (21/102) responded with a sustained and regular train of action potentials, with no, or marginal, spike-frequency adaptation (non-adapting cells, Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: The remaining R. pumilio SCN neurons (81/102) showed some degree of frequency adaptation in response to depolarizing pulses.
source: The remaining neurons (81/102) showed some degree of frequency adaptation (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B,C

claim: The proportion of R. pumilio SCN cells displaying different responses to depolarizing pulses did not vary across the day-night cycle (χ2=1.621, p=0.4447).
source: The proportion of cells displaying each of these responses did not vary across the day-night cycle (χ2=1.621, p=0.4447, Chi-square test, Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Different types of spiking behavior in R. pumilio SCN neurons likely reflect 'hardwired' differences between SCN neurons, rather than time-of-day-dependent variations in physiological state.
source: This suggests that, as in the mouse SCN (Belle et al., 2009; Belle and Piggins, 2017), these different types of spiking behavior likely reflect 'hardwired' differences between SCN neurons, rather than time-of-day-dependent variations in physiological state.
evidence: Inference from experimental data and comparison with citations to Belle et al., 2009; Belle and Piggins, 2017

claim: 67% (69/103) of R. pumilio SCN neurons immediately resumed normal firing or showed rebound depolarization spiking upon termination of hyperpolarizing pulses.
source: Upon pulse termination, 67% (69/103) of R. pumilio SCN neurons immediately resumed normal firing or showed rebound depolarization spiking before resuming normal pre-pulse level of firing (Figure 3E), as previously reported for mouse and rat SCN (Thomson and West, 1990; Pennartz et al., 1998; Kuhlman and McMahon, 2004; Belle et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and citations to Thomson and West, 1990; Pennartz et al., 1998; Kuhlman and McMahon, 2004; Belle et al., 2009

claim: 33% (34/103) of R. pumilio SCN neurons displayed a low-threshold spike (LTS) followed by a rebound hyperpolarization which produced a prominent delay (ranging from 160 to 1430 ms) before firing resumed.
source: The remaining 33% (34/103) of units displayed a low-threshold spike (LTS) followed by a rebound hyperpolarization which produced a prominent delay, ranging from 160 to 1430 ms, before firing resumed (Figures 3Fi–ii and 6H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3Fi-ii and 6H

claim: 73.5% (25/34) of R. pumilio SCN neurons with delay-to-fire responses also showed an inward rectification or depolarization 'sag' during the hyperpolarizing pulse.
source: A high proportion of cells in this second group (73.5%; 25/34) also showed an inward rectification or depolarization 'sag' (Figure 3F) during the pulse, an electrical response that is associated with H-current activation (IH, [Pennartz et al., 1998; Atkinson et al., 2011]).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and citations to Pennartz et al., 1998; Atkinson et al., 2011

claim: The hyperpolarization-evoked delay to fire and LTS response have not previously been reported for SCN neurons.
source: The hyperpolarization-evoked delay to fire and LTS response (Figure 3Fi–ii) have not previously been reported for SCN neurons, and thus represents another significant point of divergence in SCN neurophysiology between R. pumilio and, previously studied, nocturnal species.
evidence: Statement about the novelty of the finding based on literature review

claim: The relative abundance of Type-A and -B cells in R. pumilio SCN did not change across the day-night cycle (χ2=0.6552, p=0.4183).
source: The relative abundance of Type-A and -B cells did not change across the day-night cycle (χ2=0.6552, p=0.4183, Chi-square test, Figure 3G), indicating that these response properties are determined by cell-type rather than time-of-day.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and data shown in Figure 3G

claim: Non-adapting and adapting R. pumilio SCN neurons exhibited similar proportions of rebound or delay-to-fire behaviors (~34–38% delay and ~62–66% rebound).
source: In addition, analysis of the relationship between cellular responses to depolarizing and hyperpolarizing pulses revealed that non-adapting and adapting neurons exhibited similar proportions of rebound or delay-to-fire behaviors (~34–38% delay and ~62–66% rebound), suggesting that non-adapting or adapting responses in these neurons do not determine firing characteristics to hyperpolarizing pulses.
evidence: Supported by analysis of experimental data

claim: The data assimilation algorithm reproduced the voltage trajectory and nuances of action potentials and subthreshold electrical activity generated during spontaneous and evoked firing of R. pumilio SCN neurons in remarkable detail.
source: This modeling approach reproduced the voltage trajectory and nuances of action potentials and subthreshold electrical activity generated during spontaneous and evoked firing of SCN neurons in remarkable detail (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Supported by modeling results shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: The overall profile of how ionic currents contribute to AP generation is similar between R. pumilio and mouse SCN.
source: We found that the overall profile of how these currents contribute to AP generation is similar across the two species (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by modeling results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3

claim: The types of bifurcations at the transitions between rest states and spiking are the same in both R. pumilio and mouse SCN models.
source: In addition, the types of bifurcations at the transitions between rest states and spiking are the same in both models (subcritical Hopf from hyperpolarized silent to spiking, and supercritical Hopf from depolarized-silent to spiking), suggesting the qualitative dynamics that lead to repetitive AP firing are similar across the two species (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: Supported by modeling results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4A

claim: The R. pumilio model can produce all the electrical behaviors observed across the day-night cycle through an antiphase circadian rhythm in sodium and potassium leak currents.
source: Furthermore, the R. pumilio model can produce all the electrical behaviors observed across the day-night cycle (depolarized-silent, DLAMOs, fast-firing, slow-firing, and hyperpolarized-silent, Figure 4—figure supplement 4B–F) through an antiphase circadian rhythm in sodium and potassium leak currents (with higher sodium leak current during the day than at night), consistent with the 'bicycle model' proposed for the circadian regulation of electrical activity in mice and flies (Flourakis et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by modeling results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4B-F and citation to Flourakis et al., 2015

claim: Frequency adaptation in R. pumilio SCN neurons in response to excitation resulted from the progressive inactivation of sodium channels.
source: Our models revealed that frequency adaptation in SCN neurons in response to excitation resulted from the progressive inactivation of sodium channels.
evidence: Supported by modeling results

claim: The adapting-firing model indicated a much smaller amount of INa available for the APs during the depolarizing pulse (peak INa = -80pA) compared with the non-adapting model (peak INa = −580 pA).
source: Indeed, the adapting-firing model indicated a much smaller amount of INa available for the APs during the depolarizing pulse (peak INa = -80pA, Figure 5Cii), and a greater reduction in sodium conductance GNa (26 nS before vs 1.5 nS during the pulse, Figure 5Dii) compared with the non-adapting model (peak INa = −580 pA; GNa = 27 nS before vs 13 nS during the pulse, Figure 5Ci,Di).
evidence: Supported by modeling results shown in Figure 5C-D

claim: Increased sodium channel inactivation in adapting-firing neurons could not be ascribed to intrinsic differences in the sodium channel properties themselves.
source: Remarkably, however, increased sodium channel inactivation (hNa close to 0) could not be ascribed to intrinsic differences in the sodium channel properties themselves between the non-adapting and adapting-firing models as the kinetic parameters of the sodium activation and inactivation gating variables were similar (Figure 5F–G).
evidence: Supported by modeling results shown in Figure 5F-G

claim: The difference in sodium channel inactivation between adapting and non-adapting neurons was due to differing properties of the potassium channels.
source: Rather, the difference was due to differing properties of the potassium channels.
evidence: Inference from modeling results

claim: In the Type-A R. pumilio SCN neuron model, the INa and ICa currents were larger during the first AP immediately following the hyperpolarizing pulse than during the APs before the pulse.
source: Model analysis showed that in the Type-A cell, the INa and ICa currents were larger during the first AP immediately following the pulse than during the APs before the pulse (Figure 6D), leading to a high-amplitude rebound spike.
evidence: Supported by modeling results shown in Figure 6D

claim: The rebound spiking in Type-A neurons was due to sodium and calcium ion channels becoming completely de-inactivated at the hyperpolarized membrane potential reached during the pulse.
source: The rebound spiking was due to sodium and calcium ion channels becoming completely de-inactivated (hNa and hCa both approach 1) at the hyperpolarized membrane potential reached during the pulse (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by modeling results shown in Figure 6F

claim: The expanded model with IA and IH currents revealed a larger IA current during the first APs after the delay (480 pA) than during a typical spike (220 pA) in Type-B neurons.
source: The expanded model revealed a larger IA current during the first APs after the delay (480 pA) than during a typical spike (220 pA, Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by modeling results shown in Figure 6E

claim: There was 15 pA of IA current flowing during the delay itself in Type-B neurons, which was greater than the 5 pA of IA current that flows during the inter-spike interval.
source: Importantly, there was also 15 pA of IA current flowing during the delay itself (Figure 6E inset). It is noteworthy that this was greater than the 5 pA of IA current that flows during the inter-spike interval.
evidence: Supported by modeling results shown in Figure 6E

claim: The enhanced IA current following the pulse in Type-B neurons was due to de-inactivation of the A-type channel during the hyperpolarizing pulse.
source: This enhanced IA current following the pulse was due to de-inactivation of the A-type channel (hA approaches 1) during the hyperpolarizing pulse (Figure 6G), rendering the IA channel fully available upon release of the pulse, an observation that is consistent with experimental findings (Burdakov et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by modeling results shown in Figure 6G and citation to Burdakov et al., 2004

claim: Bath application of 5 mM 4-AP reversibly eliminated the rebound hyperpolarization and prominent delay-to-fire in all Type B R. pumilio SCN neurons tested (F(2, 10) = 14.09, p=0.0012).
source: As predicted, 5 mM 4-AP reversibly eliminated the rebound hyperpolarization and prominent delay-to-fire in all Type B neurons tested, irrespective of the delay duration (F(2, 10) = 14.09, p=0.0012, one way RM-ANOVA, n=6), reducing the average latency to the first spike after a 1 s −30 pA pulse from 0.596 ± 0.134 s to 0.086 ± 0.013 s (Baseline vs 4-AP, p=0.0024 Tukey's multiple comparisons test).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis

claim: By varying the maximal IA conductance and inactivation time constant parameters in the model, the full range of latency to fire seen in Type-B cells could be captured.
source: By varying the maximal IA conductance (Figure 6M,O) and inactivation time constant (Figure 6N,P) parameters, we were able to capture the full range of latency to fire seen in Type-B cells, with higher conductances and longer inactivation time constants producing longer delays.
evidence: Supported by modeling results shown in Figure 6M-P

claim: Complete removal of the IA conductance in the model eliminated the delay and produced a Type-A response.
source: Consistent with our experiments, complete removal of the IA conductance eliminated the delay and produced a Type-A response (Figure 6Oi–iii), reinforcing the different ionic composition of these two cell types.
evidence: Supported by modeling results shown in Figure 6Oi-iii

claim: IA led to a suppression of spontaneous firing rate in model R. pumilio SCN neurons in the absence of GABAergic synaptic conductance.
source: Our simulations showed that overall, in the absence of GABAergic synaptic conductance (gSyn-I = 0 nS), IA led to a suppression of spontaneous firing rate in model SCN neurons (Figure 7A,B a1 vs a4).
evidence: Supported by modeling results shown in Figure 7A,B

claim: The suppressive effect of IA on firing rate was retained following inclusion of synaptic input of either polarity.
source: This effect was retained following inclusion of synaptic input of either polarity (Figure 7A–B, compare a2 vs a5, and a3 vs a6), with the suppressive effect of gsyn-I especially augmented by high IA (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by modeling results shown in Figure 7A-B

claim: The weight of the imposed suppression of firing by IA conductances was stronger at night (in hyperpolarized low-firing neurons) than in the day (in more depolarized fast-firing neurons).
source: In our model, the weight of the imposed suppression of firing by IA conductances was stronger at night (in hyperpolarized low-firing neurons) than in the day (in more depolarized fast-firing neurons) (Figure 7).
evidence: Supported by modeling results shown in Figure 7

claim: The fundamental daily rhythm in electrical excitability ('upstate' during the day and a 'downstate' at night) reported for nocturnal species is retained in R. pumilio.
source: Most importantly, the fundamental daily rhythm in electrical excitability ('upstate' during the day and a 'downstate' at night [Allen et al., 2017; Belle and Diekman, 2018; Harvey et al., 2020]) reported for nocturnal species is retained in R. pumilio.
evidence: Inference from experimental data and comparison with citations to Allen et al., 2017; Belle and Diekman, 2018; Harvey et al., 2020

claim: The response of R. pumilio SCN neurons to depolarizing inputs and the underlying ionic mechanisms were similar to that of nocturnal rodents.
source: Moreover, the response of R. pumilio SCN neurons to depolarizing inputs and the underlying ionic mechanisms were similar to that of nocturnal rodents (Belle et al., 2009).
evidence: Inference from experimental and modeling data and comparison with citation to Belle et al., 2009

claim: A substantial fraction of R. pumilio neurons showed a prominent delay-to-fire (for several hundreds of milliseconds in some cells) following inhibitory pulses.
source: Thus, we found that a substantial fraction of R. pumilio neurons showed a prominent delay-to-fire (for several hundreds of milliseconds in some cells) following inhibitory pulses.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: The delay-to-fire response to inhibition has been observed in neurons elsewhere in the brain but has never before been reported in SCN neurons.
source: This sort of electrical reaction to inhibition has been observed in neurons elsewhere in the brain (Schoppa and Westbrook, 1999; Saito and Isa, 2000; Burdakov and Ashcroft, 2002; Burdakov et al., 2004; Nadin and Pfaffinger, 2010; Tarfa et al., 2017), but to the best of our knowledge has never before been reported in SCN neurons (Thomson and West, 1990; Pennartz et al., 1998; Kuhlman and McMahon, 2004; Belle et al., 2009; Gamble et al., 2011; Belle and Piggins, 2017).
evidence: Supported by literature review with citations to Schoppa and Westbrook, 1999; Saito and Isa, 2000; Burdakov and Ashcroft, 2002; Burdakov et al., 2004; Nadin and Pfaffinger, 2010; Tarfa et al., 2017; Thomson and West, 1990; Pennartz et al., 1998; Kuhlman and McMahon, 2004; Belle et al., 2009; Gamble et al., 2011; Belle and Piggins, 2017

claim: Computational models and experimental findings identified the activity of the transient subthreshold A-type potassium channels (IA) as the determinant of the delay-to-fire response in R. pumilio SCN neurons.
source: Our computational models and experimental findings identified the activity of the transient subthreshold A-type potassium channels (IA) as the determinant of this suppressive bioelectrical effect, with the IA conductance density (which presumably represents the number of functional IA channels), defining the delay-to-fire latency.
evidence: Supported by modeling and experimental data

claim: The pore-forming (α) subunits of IA channels (Kv1.4, 4.1, 4.2 and 4.3) are present in nocturnal rodent (rat, mouse and hamster) SCN neurons.
source: The pore-forming (α) subunits of IA channels (Kv1.4, 4.1, 4.2 and 4.3) are present in nocturnal rodent (rat, mouse and hamster) SCN neurons, and have been implicated in regulating electrical activity and supporting core clock function (Huang et al., 1993; Bouskila and Dudek, 1995; Alvado and Allen, 2008; Itri et al., 2010; Granados-Fuentes et al., 2012; Granados-Fuentes et al., 2015; Hermanstyne et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Huang et al., 1993; Bouskila and Dudek, 1995; Alvado and Allen, 2008; Itri et al., 2010; Granados-Fuentes et al., 2012; Granados-Fuentes et al., 2015; Hermanstyne et al., 2017

claim: The IA inactivation time constant measured in mouse and hamster SCN neurons showed relatively fast gating variables (below 22 ms).
source: Interestingly, the IA inactivation time constant measured in mouse and hamster SCN neurons showed relatively fast gating variables (below 22 ms: [Alvado and Allen, 2008; Itri et al., 2010]), consistent, therefore, with the presence of rebound but not delay-to-fire characteristics in SCN neurons of these species.
evidence: Supported by citations to Alvado and Allen, 2008; Itri et al., 2010

claim: To fully model the range of delay-to-fire behaviors observed in R. pumilio SCN neurons, the original mouse model had to be supplemented with IA channels with a slow inactivation time constant (near 140 ms).
source: In agreement, to fully model the range of delay-to-fire behaviors observed in R. pumilio SCN neurons, our original mouse model had to be supplemented with IA channels with a slow inactivation time constant (near 140 ms) (Figure 6C,O,P).
evidence: Supported by modeling results shown in Figure 6C,O,P

claim: The functional properties of the IA channel family (Kv4), specifically inactivation time constant and current density, can be influenced by two classes of auxiliary proteins known as Kv channel-interacting proteins (KChIP1–4) and dipeptidyl peptidase-like proteins (DPLPs; DPP6 and DPP10).
source: The functional properties of the IA channel family (Kv4), specifically inactivation time constant and current density, can be influenced by two classes of auxiliary proteins known as Kv channel-interacting proteins (KChIP1–4) and dipeptidyl peptidase-like proteins (DPLPs; DPP6 and DPP10) (Jerng and Pfaffinger, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jerng and Pfaffinger, 2014

claim: When associated with various complements of KChIP and DPLP proteins, the IA channel inactivation time constant can vary from a few ms to several hundred ms.
source: When associated with the various complements of these proteins, the IA channel inactivation time constant can vary from a few ms to several hundred ms (depending on their expression pattern and the nature of interaction with the channels), reversibly transforming rebound firing to delay firing cells (Shibata et al., 2000; Holmqvist et al., 2002; Jerng et al., 2004; Jerng et al., 2005; Jerng et al., 2007; Amarillo et al., 2008; Maffie et al., 2009; Nadin and Pfaffinger, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shibata et al., 2000; Holmqvist et al., 2002; Jerng et al., 2004; Jerng et al., 2005; Jerng et al., 2007; Amarillo et al., 2008; Maffie et al., 2009; Nadin and Pfaffinger, 2010

claim: The transcripts for KChIP and DPLP auxiliary proteins are expressed brain-wide across different mammals, including in the SCN of nocturnal rodents and the diurnal baboon.
source: The transcripts for these auxiliary proteins are expressed brain-wide across different mammals, including in the SCN of nocturnal rodents (Wen et al., 2020) and the diurnal baboon (Mure et al., 2018), and have been implicated in circadian control mechanisms in other excitable cell types (Jeyaraj et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wen et al., 2020; Mure et al., 2018; Jeyaraj et al., 2012

claim: IA auxiliary proteins are known to regulate the input resistance (Rinput) of neurons without changing resting membrane potential (RMP) and capacitance.
source: These IA auxiliary proteins are known to regulate the input resistance (Rinput) of neurons without changing resting membrane potential (RMP) and capacitance (Nadin and Pfaffinger, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nadin and Pfaffinger, 2010

claim: Variation in KChIP and DPLP activity across the population of R. pumilio SCN neurons could both produce diversity in delay-to-fire activity and disrupt the link between RMP and Rinput across neurons observed in nocturnal species.
source: Thus, variation in KChIP and DPLP activity across the population of R. pumilio SCN neurons could both produce diversity in delay-to-fire activity and disrupt the link between RMP and Rinput across neurons observed in nocturnal species (Kuhlman and McMahon, 2004; Belle et al., 2009).
evidence: Speculation based on modeling results and comparison with citations to Kuhlman and McMahon, 2004; Belle et al., 2009

claim: IA channels can suppress spontaneous firing rate in nocturnal SCN and elsewhere in the brain.
source: Experimental results in nocturnal SCN (Granados-Fuentes et al., 2012; Hermanstyne et al., 2017) and elsewhere in the brain (Connor and Stevens, 1971; Rudy, 1988; Liss et al., 2001; Baranauskas, 2007; Khaliq and Bean, 2008) reveal that IA channels can suppress spontaneous firing rate.
evidence: Supported by citations to Granados-Fuentes et al., 2012; Hermanstyne et al., 2017; Connor and Stevens, 1971; Rudy, 1988; Liss et al., 2001; Baranauskas, 2007; Khaliq and Bean, 2008

claim: Modeling revealed that IA reduced the effect of intrinsic or synaptically-driven increases in excitability on firing, while enhancing the impact of inhibitory currents.
source: Our modeling returned a similar impact of IA in R. pumilio, while revealing aspects of this effect that could be especially relevant for a diurnal species. Thus, in general, IA reduced the effect of intrinsic or synaptically-driven increases in excitability on firing, while enhancing the impact of inhibitory currents (Figure 7).
evidence: Supported by modeling results shown in Figure 7

claim: The biophysical properties of IA channels, together with its sensitivity to neurotransmitters, could provide an opportunity for the R. pumilio SCN to compensate for the reduction in inhibitory inputs at night.
source: The biophysical properties of IA channels (conductance active at the subthreshold range of the RMP and progressively becoming available with hyperpolarization), together with its sensitivity to neurotransmitters (Aghajanian, 1985; Yang et al., 2001; Burdakov and Ashcroft, 2002), could provide an opportunity for the R. pumilio SCN to compensate for the reduction in inhibitory inputs at night.
evidence: Speculation based on modeling results and citations to Aghajanian, 1985; Yang et al., 2001; Burdakov and Ashcroft, 2002

claim: The ability of IA to reduce the impact of excitatory inputs would apply an appropriate 'brake' on daytime activity of the SCN.
source: The ability of IA to reduce the impact of such excitatory inputs, and perhaps augment the effect of inhibitory inputs from the thalamus, lateral hypothalamus or retina (Belle et al., 2014; Sonoda et al., 2020) or intrinsic to the SCN (Hannibal et al., 2010), would apply an appropriate 'brake' on daytime activity of the SCN.
evidence: Speculation based on modeling results and citations to Belle et al., 2014; Sonoda et al., 2020; Hannibal et al., 2010

claim: In the mouse SCN, increased membrane resistance is associated with depolarized RMP during the day, and at night hyperpolarized cells exhibit reduced membrane resistance.
source: In the mouse SCN, increased membrane resistance is associated with depolarized RMP during the day, and at night hyperpolarized cells exhibit reduced membrane resistance (Kuhlman and McMahon, 2004; Belle et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kuhlman and McMahon, 2004; Belle et al., 2009

claim: In the R. pumilio SCN, RMP is more depolarized during the day than at night, but there is not a significant day-night difference in membrane resistance.
source: In the R. pumilio SCN, we found that RMP is more depolarized during the day than at night as in the mouse SCN, but that there is not a significant day-night difference in membrane resistance (Figure 2F) due to a subset of day cells with relatively low Rinput (despite a depolarized RMP) and a subset of night cells with relatively high Rinput (despite a hyperpolarized RMP).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F

claim: The decoupling of membrane potential and input resistance in the R. pumilio SCN could reflect the activity and magnitude of different conductances in this species compared to mouse SCN.
source: The decoupling of membrane potential and input resistance in the R. pumilio SCN could reflect the activity and magnitude of different conductances in this species compared to mouse SCN.
evidence: Speculation based on experimental observations

claim: In R. pumilio, cells with high membrane resistance during the night may provide an additional cellular mechanism to amplify inhibitory signals.
source: In R. pumilio, cells with high membrane resistance during the night therefore may provide an additional cellular mechanism to amplify inhibitory signals.
evidence: Speculation based on experimental observations and known principles of neuronal physiology

claim: During the day, depolarized R. pumilio SCN cells with low membrane resistance would be less sensitive to excitatory inputs.
source: During the day, depolarized cells with low membrane resistance would be less sensitive to excitatory inputs, thereby supporting the daytime 'brake' in extrinsic excitability.
evidence: Speculation based on experimental observations and known principles of neuronal physiology

claim: The data assimilation algorithm was able to reliably perform state and parameter estimation for R. pumilio SCN neuron models from current-clamp recordings without the use of voltage-clamp and pharmacological agents to isolate specific currents.
source: Our state-of-the-art DA algorithm was able to reliably perform state and parameter estimation for R. pumilio SCN neuron models from current-clamp recordings without the use of voltage-clamp and pharmacological agents to isolate specific currents, and without the injection of custom-designed stimulus waveforms as used in other DA approaches (Meliza et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement about the methodology and comparison with citation to Meliza et al., 2014
